correctness.rationale: Multiplicativity gives \(\sigma^*(p^a q)-\sigma^{(e)}(p^a q)=1+p^a-q\Delta_a(p)\), \(\Delta_a(p)=\sum_{d\mid a,\ d<a}p^d-1\). The exact integer inequality and finite prime-counting formula follow. With d=max proper divisor of a and b=a-d, the cutoff is \(p^b(1+O_a(1/p))\). Replacing it incurs at most \(O_a(T^b+T)\) for \(T=X^{1/(a+b)}\). The prime number theorem and partial summation yield lower-range constant \(1/[b(b+1)]\) and upper-range constant \(1/[b(a-1)]\) in units \(T^{b+1}/(\log T)^2\); the upper tail is negligible by a two-stage bound. Excluding \(p=q\) is also lower-order. The rational K values and exact inequalities were checked from packaged verify.py for \(2\le a\le6\) at three finite X values. There is no extrapolation from finite data.

originality.rationale: The published motivating work treats ambient natural density, upper bounds and the equality question; it does not assert the all-fixed-exponent asymptotic. Inspected published records on exact equality through exponent 49 and a lower bound on ambient density have mathematically distinct conclusions and do not imply a positive-count asymptotic on the sparse \(p^a q\) strata. RSA-prime ratio results concern pq, not the divisor comparison on \(p^a q\). Searches for exponent threshold, prime-product estimates, exact tables and equivalent formulations found no covering formula. Prime number theorem methodology is standard and not claimed as new. value.rationale: The original work asks for quantitative understanding of the comparison of unitary and exponential divisor sums. The fixed exponent layers \(p^a q\) are the simplest non-squarefree strata where the local factors pull in opposite directions. Rather than a small finite enumeration or a formal rephrasing, the claim gives every fixed exponent a precise infinite asymptotic, an explicit constant, and a growth exponent controlled by the divisor lattice of a; it also proves relative density zero inside each sparse stratum despite positive ambient density. This answers a natural conditional counting question and provides a checkable framework for comparisons in more complicated exponent patterns, without claiming to solve the original global density problem.
